1:1.t: Isaiah prophesied in Judah from about 740 to 700 BC, under the four kings named.

1:8.t: "A hut in a cucumber field": the KJV's "a lodge in a garden of cucumbers", a temporary shelter for a watchman, left standing alone after harvest.

1:13.t: "I cannot bear wickedness together with a solemn assembly": the KJV's "I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting".

1:17.t: "Correct the oppressor": the KJV's "relieve the oppressed". The Hebrew can be read either way.

1:25.t: "Impurities": the KJV's "tin", the base metal separated from silver in refining.

1:27.t: "Those in her who repent": the KJV's "her converts", literally "those who return".

1:29.t: "Sacred oaks ... gardens": places of idol worship.

2:2.t: Micah 4:1-3 contains nearly the same prophecy.

"The last days" (Hebrew be'acharit hayyamim): literally "at the end of the days", the future time when God completes His purposes. The New Testament says these days began with Christ (Acts 2:17, Hebrews 1:2).

2:6.t: "Make deals with foreigners": the KJV's "please themselves in the children of strangers". The Hebrew is uncertain.

2:16.t: "Every beautiful vessel": the KJV's "all pleasant pictures". The Hebrew sekhiyyot is uncertain.

3:2.t: "The diviner": the KJV's "the prudent"; the Hebrew qosem usually means a diviner, here one of the leaders the people relied on.

3:17.t: "Make their scalps bald": the KJV's "discover their secret parts". The Hebrew is uncertain.

3:18.t: Several of these items of jewelry and clothing cannot be identified with certainty.

3:24.t: "Branding": the KJV's "burning", perhaps the branding of captives.

4:5.t: "Canopy": the KJV's "defence"; Hebrew chuppah, a covering or wedding canopy.

5:7.t: "Justice ... bloodshed; righteousness ... cries of distress": a wordplay in Hebrew: mishpat / mispach and tsedaqah / tse'aqah.

5:10.t: "About four hectares": the KJV's "ten acres", literally "ten yoke", the land ten teams of oxen plow in a day. "About twenty-two liters of wine": the KJV's "one bath". "Two hundred twenty liters ... twenty-two liters": the KJV's "the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah".

6:13.t: "Terebinth": the KJV's "teil tree". The KJV reads "But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten".

7:2.t: Ephraim, the leading tribe, stands for the northern kingdom of Israel.

7:15.t: "Curds": the KJV's "butter", a thick, soured milk.

7:23.t: "A thousand pieces of silver": the KJV's "a thousand silverlings"; the Hebrew does not name the unit.

8:1.t: Maher-shalal-hash-baz means "quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil".

8:6.t: Shiloah: the channel carrying water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem, a picture of the LORD's quiet care.

8:14.t: Paul and Peter apply this passage to Christ (Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:8).

8:19.t: "Mediums and spiritists": the KJV's "them that have familiar spirits, and ... wizards".

8:20.t: "No light of dawn": the KJV's "there is no light in them". In the Hebrew 8:23 is 9:1.

9:1.t: The KJV reads "the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted ... and afterward did more grievously afflict her". In the Hebrew this verse is 8:23, and 9:1-21 is 9:2-21. Matthew 4:13-16 sees this fulfilled when Jesus began His ministry in Galilee.

9:2.t: "Deep darkness": the KJV's "the shadow of death".

9:5.t: "Every warrior's boot ... will be burned": the KJV reads "every battle of the warrior is with confused noise ... but this shall be with burning".

10:21.t: "A remnant will return": Hebrew she'ar yashuv, the name of Isaiah's son (7:3).

10:22.t: Paul quotes these verses in Romans 9:27-28.

10:27.t: "Because of the anointing": the KJV's reading; the Hebrew is difficult and may mean "because of fatness".

10:28.t: The towns trace the Assyrian army's march from the north toward Jerusalem.

11:11.t: "Lower Egypt ... Upper Egypt ... Babylonia": the KJV's "Egypt ... Pathros ... Shinar".

12:2.t: "The LORD, Yahweh": the KJV's "the LORD JEHOVAH", Hebrew Yah YHWH. Compare Exodus 15:2.

13:1.t: "A prophecy": the KJV's "The burden", Hebrew massa, a weighty message, usually of judgment. Chapters 13-23 are prophecies against the nations.

13:12.t: Ophir: a region famous for fine gold (1 Kings 9:28).

13:21.t: "Jackals ... ostriches ... wild goats ... hyenas": the KJV's "doleful creatures ... owls ... satyrs ... wild beasts of the islands ... dragons". Several of these animals are uncertain; the Hebrew se'irim ("wild goats", the KJV's "satyrs") may also mean goat-demons.

14:4.t: "His fury": the KJV's "the golden city"; the Hebrew madhebah is uncertain.

14:9.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "Hell", Hebrew Sheol. 14:11 "The grave" is also Sheol.
"Spirits of the departed": Hebrew rephaim; see Job 26:5.

14:15.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "Hell", Hebrew Sheol. 14:11 "The grave" is also Sheol.

14:23.t: "Owls": the KJV's "the bittern"; the bird is uncertain.

15:2.t: "Dibon goes up to its temple": the KJV's "He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon". Bajith means "house" or "temple".

15:5.t: "Eglath Shelishiyah": the KJV's "an heifer of three years old"; it is probably a place name.

15:7.t: "Ravine of the Willows": the KJV's "the brook of the willows".

15:9.t: Dimon is probably Dibon, with a wordplay on dam, "blood".

16:1.t: Moab was famous for its sheep and paid tribute in lambs (2 Kings 3:4). Sela was in Edom.

16:7.t: "Raisin cakes": the KJV's "foundations"; the Hebrew ashishe can mean either.

16:14.t: "As a hired worker counts the years": a hired worker serves exactly the agreed time and no more.

17:8.t: "Asherah poles": the KJV's "groves", wooden poles honoring the goddess Asherah.

18:1.t: Cush: the region south of Egypt, the KJV's "Ethiopia". "Whirring wings": the KJV's "shadowing with wings", perhaps insects or sailing ships.

18:2.t: "Tall and smooth-skinned ... aggressive": the KJV's "scattered and peeled ... meted out and trodden down". The Hebrew words are rare and uncertain.

19:5.t: "The river ... the Nile": the KJV's "the river ... the brooks"; the Hebrew ye'or is the Nile.

19:10.t: "The workers in cloth": the KJV reads "all that make sluices and ponds for fish". The Hebrew is uncertain.

19:13.t: Zoan and Memphis (the KJV's "Noph") were royal cities of Egypt.

19:18.t: "The City of Destruction": the KJV's reading and the standard Hebrew (ha-heres). Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Dead Sea Scrolls read ha-cheres, "the City of the Sun", that is, Heliopolis.

20:1.t: "The supreme commander": the KJV's "Tartan", an Assyrian title rather than a name. Ashdod fell in 711 BC.

20:2.t: "Stripped": the KJV's "naked"; he wore no outer garment, like a captive.

21:1.t: "The Desert by the Sea": Babylon, in the marshy plain near the Persian Gulf. "The Negev": the KJV's "the south".

21:2.t: Elam and Media joined the Persians who conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

21:11.t: Dumah means "silence"; it is also a place in Arabia. Seir is in Edom.

22:1.t: "The Valley of Vision": Jerusalem, the place where God revealed Himself to the prophets.

22:8.t: "The Palace of the Forest": Solomon's armory, built of cedars of Lebanon (1 Kings 7:2, 10:17).

22:9.t: Hezekiah prepared Jerusalem for siege by storing water and strengthening the walls (2 Chronicles 32:2-5).

22:13.t: Paul quotes "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" in 1 Corinthians 15:32.

23:3.t: Shihor: a branch of the Nile.

23:13.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

24:1.t: Chapters 24-27, sometimes called "the Isaiah apocalypse", describe God's judgment on the whole earth and His final victory.

24:4.t: "The heavens": the KJV's "the haughty people of the earth"; the Hebrew marom can mean either "height" or "the exalted".

24:15.t: "In the east": the KJV's "in the fires", Hebrew urim, "the regions of light".

25:6.t: "Aged wine ... the finest of wines": the KJV's "wines on the lees ... well refined", wine left to mature on its sediment.

26:4.t: "The LORD, Yahweh": the KJV's "the LORD JEHOVAH", Hebrew Yah YHWH. "The Rock eternal": the KJV's "everlasting strength", literally "a rock of ages".

26:19.t: "Your dew is like the dew of the morning": the KJV's "the dew of herbs". The Hebrew orot may mean "lights" or "herbs".
"Your dead will live ... their bodies will rise": one of the clearest Old Testament promises of bodily resurrection, together with Daniel 12:2.

27:2.t: "A fruitful vineyard": the KJV's "A vineyard of red wine". Some Hebrew manuscripts read "a delightful vineyard". This song reverses the Song of the Vineyard in 5:1-7.

27:8.t: "By warfare and exile": the KJV's "In measure, when it shooteth forth". The Hebrew is obscure.

27:12.t: "The Euphrates ... the Wadi of Egypt": the KJV's "the river ... the stream of Egypt", the borders of the promised land.

28:1.t: Samaria, the capital of Ephraim (the northern kingdom), stood on a hill above a fertile valley like a wreath on a drinker's head.

28:10.t: "Do this, do that, a rule for this, a rule for that": the KJV's "precept upon precept ... line upon line". The Hebrew tsav latsav tsav latsav, qav laqav qav laqav sounds like baby talk; the drunken leaders mock Isaiah's teaching as fit for infants.

28:13.t: "Do this, do that, a rule for this, a rule for that": the KJV's "precept upon precept ... line upon line". The Hebrew tsav latsav tsav latsav, qav laqav qav laqav sounds like baby talk; the drunken leaders mock Isaiah's teaching as fit for infants.

28:15.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell", Hebrew Sheol.

28:18.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell", Hebrew Sheol.

28:21.t: Mount Perazim and the Valley of Gibeon: places of God's victories for David (2 Samuel 5:20-25, 1 Chronicles 14:16). His "strange work" now is judgment on His own people.

28:25.t: "Caraway": the KJV's "fitches", probably black cumin. "Spelt": the KJV's "rie".

28:27.t: "Caraway": the KJV's "fitches", probably black cumin. "Spelt": the KJV's "rie".

29:1.t: "Ariel": a name for Jerusalem, meaning either "lion of God" or "altar hearth" (Ezekiel 43:15-16).

29:4.t: "Ghostlike": the KJV's "as of one that hath a familiar spirit".

30:4.t: Zoan and Hanes were cities in Egypt.

30:7.t: "Rahab the Do-Nothing": the KJV's "Their strength is to sit still". Rahab, a sea monster, was a name for Egypt (Psalm 87:4).

30:24.t: "Fork and shovel": the KJV's "the shovel and ... the fan", tools for winnowing grain.

30:33.t: "Topheth": the place in the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned to Molech (2 Kings 23:10); here a funeral pyre prepared for the Assyrian king.

31:8.t: "By no human sword": fulfilled when the angel of the LORD struck down the Assyrian army (37:36).

33:9.t: "The Arabah": the KJV's "a wilderness", the dry rift valley south of the Dead Sea.

33:18.t: "Where is that chief officer?": the KJV's "Where is the scribe? where is the receiver?" Paul echoes this verse in 1 Corinthians 1:20.

34:5.t: Edom (the KJV's "Idumea") stands for all the nations hostile to God's people. Bozrah was its chief city.

34:11.t: Several of these birds and animals cannot be identified with certainty. "Night creatures" (Hebrew lilit, the KJV's "screech owl") may be a night bird or a night demon.

36:1.t: Chapters 36-39 closely parallel 2 Kings 18:13-20:19; the wording here follows the translation of 2 Kings where the texts agree. Sennacherib's invasion was in 701 BC.

36:2.t: "The Rab-shakeh": an Assyrian title, "chief cupbearer" or field commander, which the KJV treats as a name.

36:11.t: "Aramaic": the KJV's "the Syrian language", the international language of diplomacy. "The language of Judah": the KJV's "the Jews' language", Hebrew.

38:8.t: "The stairway of Ahaz": the KJV's "the sun dial of Ahaz", literally "the steps (degrees) of Ahaz", perhaps a stairway used to tell time by its shadow.

38:9.t: Hezekiah's psalm of thanksgiving appears only in Isaiah, not in 2 Kings.

38:14.t: "A swift or a thrush": the KJV's "a crane or a swallow".

38:21.t: These verses complete the account of verses 1-8; compare 2 Kings 20:7-8.

39:8.t: This chapter closes the first part of Isaiah. Chapter 40 begins the message of comfort to the exiles in Babylon foretold in verses 6-7.

40:1.t: Chapters 40-66 speak comfort to God's people in exile in Babylon and beyond, promising return, the coming Servant and a new creation.

40:2.t: "Hard service": the KJV's "warfare", a term of compulsory service.

40:3.t: All four Gospels apply these verses to John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus (Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, John 1:23). The KJV's punctuation, "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness", is the reading the Gospels follow.

40:6.t: "Their faithfulness" (Hebrew chasdo): the word hesed used here of human loyalty, which is as short-lived as wildflowers, in contrast to God's word. The KJV's "goodliness".

40:12.t: "The breadth of His hand": the KJV's "the span", the distance from thumb to little finger, about 23 centimeters.

41:2.t: "One from the east ... one from the north": Cyrus the Persian, who conquered Babylon and let the exiles return (see 44:28, 45:1).

41:25.t: "One from the east ... one from the north": Cyrus the Persian, who conquered Babylon and let the exiles return (see 44:28, 45:1).

41:19.t: "Acacia": the KJV's "shittah tree". "Olive": the KJV's "oil tree". "Cypress": the KJV's "box tree".

42:11.t: Kedar: an Arabian tribe; Sela, "the rock", a city of Edom.

42:19.t: "The one in covenant with Me": the KJV's "he that is perfect". The Hebrew meshullam is related to shalom.

43:3.t: "Cush": the KJV's "Ethiopia". Seba was a land in the far south.

43:24.t: "Fragrant calamus": the KJV's "sweet cane", used in incense and anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).

43:28.t: "Destruction": Hebrew cherem, the ban of total destruction.

44:2.t: "Jeshurun": the KJV's "Jesurun", a poetic name for Israel meaning "the upright one" (Deuteronomy 32:15).

44:8.t: "No other Rock": the KJV reads "yea, there is no God"; the Hebrew is tsur, "rock".

44:9.t: A satire on idol-making: the same log that cooks a meal becomes a god.

44:28.t: Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and in 538 BC decreed that the Jews could return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1-4). Isaiah names him well over a century earlier.

45:1.t: "Strip kings of their armor": the KJV's "loose the loins of kings".
"His anointed" (Hebrew meshicho): "His messiah". Cyrus, a pagan king, is anointed in the sense of being appointed by God for a task, freeing God's people. He foreshadows the greater Anointed One.

45:24.t: The last words of the KJV verse, "is all righteousness and strength", are a marginal note in the source text, not part of the verse.

46:1.t: Bel (Marduk) and Nebo (Nabu) were chief gods of Babylon. Their images had to be carried by animals, while the LORD carries His people (verses 3-4).

46:11.t: "A bird of prey ... a man to fulfill My purpose": Cyrus.

47:1.t: "Queen city of the Chaldeans": the KJV's "daughter of the Chaldeans".

47:13.t: "Stargazers who make predictions month by month": the KJV's "the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators".

48:1.t: "The line of Judah": the KJV's "the waters of Judah".

48:14.t: "The LORD's chosen ally": the KJV's "The LORD hath loved him", Cyrus.

48:22.t: This refrain closes a section; it is repeated at 57:21.

49:12.t: "The region of Aswan": the KJV's "the land of Sinim". The Dead Sea Scrolls read Syene, modern Aswan in southern Egypt.

49:24.t: "The righteous": the KJV's "the lawful captive". The Dead Sea Scrolls and other versions read "the fierce", as in verse 25.

51:9.t: Rahab: the sea monster, a symbol of chaos and of Egypt (30:7). God's victory at the Red Sea is pictured as cutting it down.

51:22.t: "Your Sovereign LORD": the KJV's "thy Lord the LORD".

52:5.t: Paul quotes "My name is constantly blasphemed" in Romans 2:24.

52:7.t: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:15 of those who preach the gospel.

52:11.t: Paul echoes this verse in 2 Corinthians 6:17.

52:13.t: The fourth Servant Song, the Song of the Suffering Servant. It is quoted or alluded to throughout the New Testament (Matthew 8:17, Luke 22:37, John 12:38, Acts 8:32-35, Romans 10:16, 1 Peter 2:22-25).

52:14.t: "Many were appalled at Him": the KJV's "many were astonied at thee".

53:1.t: John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote this verse.

53:8.t: "Who can speak of His descendants?": the KJV's "who shall declare his generation?" The Hebrew dor may mean descendants or contemporaries.

53:11.t: "He will see the light of life": the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek read "light"; the standard Hebrew and the KJV read "He shall see of the travail of his soul".

54:1.t: Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 4:27.

54:11.t: Several of these stones are uncertain. Revelation 21:18-21 uses this picture for the new Jerusalem.

54:13.t: Jesus quotes this verse in John 6:45.

56:7.t: Jesus quotes "My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations" when He clears the temple (Mark 11:17).

57:5.t: "You burn with lust among the oaks": the KJV's "Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree".

57:6.t: "Grain offerings": the KJV's "meat offering", which in KJV English means food.

57:9.t: "Molech": the KJV's "the king"; the Hebrew melekh may be the god Molech. "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell", Hebrew Sheol.

57:19.t: Paul echoes "Peace, peace, to those far and near" in Ephesians 2:17.

59:7.t: Paul quotes these verses in Romans 3:15-17.

59:20.t: Paul quotes these verses in Romans 11:26-27, following the Greek, "The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will turn godlessness away from Jacob."

60:6.t: Midian, Ephah and Sheba were Arabian peoples known for camel caravans and trade in gold and incense. Compare Matthew 2:11.

60:7.t: Kedar and Nebaioth were Arabian tribes descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).

61:3.t: "A crown of beauty instead of ashes": a wordplay in Hebrew, pe'er (headdress) and epher (ashes).

61:8.t: "Robbery and wrongdoing": the KJV's "robbery for burnt offering"; the Hebrew be'olah can be read "with burnt offering" or "with wrongdoing".

62:4.t: "Hephzibah" means "my delight is in her"; "Beulah" means "married".

62:5.t: "Your Builder": the Hebrew banayikh may be read "your sons", as the KJV has it, or "your Builder".

63:1.t: Edom means "red"; Bozrah sounds like the Hebrew for "grape harvest". The picture is of the LORD returning from judgment, His garments red like a grape-treader's. Revelation 19:13-15 draws on this passage.

63:19.t: "We are Yours from of old; but You have not ruled over them": the KJV reads "We are thine: thou never barest rule over them". The Hebrew can also be read "We have become like those You never ruled". In the Hebrew, 64:1 is the second half of 63:19, and 64:2-12 is numbered 64:1-11.

64:5.t: "How then can we be saved?": the KJV reads "in those is continuance, and we shall be saved". The Hebrew is uncertain.

64:6.t: "Filthy rags": literally "garments of menstruation", ritually unclean cloth.

65:1.t: Paul quotes these verses in Romans 10:20-21: verse 1 of the Gentiles, verse 2 of Israel.

65:4.t: "Keeping secret vigil": the KJV's "lodge in the monuments", perhaps to consult the dead.

65:10.t: The Valley of Achor ("trouble") was where Achan was executed (Joshua 7:24-26); it will become a place of rest (Hosea 2:15).

65:11.t: "Fortune ... Destiny": the KJV's "that troop ... that number"; the Hebrew Gad and Meni are names of gods of fate.

65:20.t: "The one who dies at a hundred will be thought a mere child": the KJV's "the child shall die an hundred years old".

66:1.t: Stephen quotes these verses in Acts 7:49-50.

66:19.t: "Pul and Lud ... Tubal and Greece": distant peoples; the KJV's "Javan" is Greece.

1:4.t: "The Holy One of Israel" (Hebrew qedosh yisra'el): Isaiah's favorite title for God, used about twenty-five times in the book and only a few times elsewhere. After his vision in chapter 6, holiness is at the center of his message.

1:18.t: "Let us settle this together" (Hebrew venivvakhechah): the KJV's "let us reason together". The verb is a legal term: God summons His people to court, and then offers cleansing instead of condemnation.

2:4.t: "Settle disputes" (Hebrew hokhiach): the same legal verb as in 1:18.

4:2.t: "The Branch of the LORD" (Hebrew tsemach YHWH): a title that later prophets use for the coming Messiah from David's line (Jeremiah 23:5, Zechariah 3:8, 6:12). Here it may also refer to the land's renewed growth.

5:1.t: The Song of the Vineyard: Israel is God's vineyard. Jesus builds on this parable in Matthew 21:33-44; see also John 15:1-8.

5:16.t: "The holy God shows Himself holy" (Hebrew niqdash): God's holiness is displayed when He acts in justice.

5:25.t: "His hand is still stretched out": a refrain of judgment repeated in 9:12, 17, 21 and 10:4.

6:2.t: "Seraphim" (Hebrew seraphim): the plural of saraph, from the verb "to burn": "burning ones". The KJV's "seraphims" adds an English plural to a Hebrew plural. They are mentioned only here in the Bible.

6:3.t: "Holy, holy, holy" (Hebrew qadosh): Hebrew repeats a word to express the highest degree; threefold repetition is unique. Holiness means God's utter separateness from all that is common or sinful. Revelation 4:8 echoes the song.

6:7.t: "Your sin atoned for" (Hebrew tekhuppar): the verb kipper, used of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The coal from the altar of sacrifice cleanses the prophet.

6:8.t: "Who will go for Us?": God speaks in the plural, as in Genesis 1:26. Christian readers see a hint of the Trinity; John 12:41 says Isaiah saw Christ's glory.

6:9.t: Jesus quotes these verses to explain why many did not understand His parables (Matthew 13:14-15), and Paul uses them at the end of Acts (Acts 28:26-27).

7:9.t: "If you do not stand firm in your faith, you will not stand at all": a wordplay in Hebrew, ta'aminu / te'amenu, both from aman, "to be firm, to believe", the root of "amen". The KJV's "If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established."

7:14.t: "The virgin" (Hebrew ha'almah): almah means a young woman of marriageable age. It is never used of a married woman in the Bible. The Greek translation, made before Christ, rendered it parthenos, "virgin", and Matthew 1:23 quotes that reading of the birth of Jesus. The KJV's "a virgin" is kept. "Immanuel" means "God with us" (see 8:8, 8:10).

9:6.t: The names of the Child: "Wonderful Counselor" (pele yo'ets), a counselor whose plans are a wonder; "Mighty God" (el gibbor), the same title used of the LORD in 10:21; "Everlasting Father" (avi'ad), a father to His people forever; "Prince of Peace" (sar shalom). The KJV separates "Wonderful, Counsellor". Christians have long read these names as fulfilled in Jesus (Luke 1:32-33). Following this reading, the pronouns for the Child are capitalized.

11:1.t: "A shoot ... from the stump of Jesse": David's royal family will be cut down like a tree, but a new King will sprout from its stump. "Branch" (Hebrew netser) may lie behind Matthew 2:23, "He will be called a Nazarene".

11:2.t: "The Spirit of the LORD" (Hebrew ruach YHWH): the Messiah is anointed with God's Spirit (see 61:1, Luke 4:18, Matthew 3:16).

11:10.t: Paul quotes this verse from the Greek in Romans 15:12 to show that the nations will hope in Christ.

14:12.t: "Morning star, son of the dawn" (Hebrew helel ben-shachar): helel means "shining one", the morning star (Venus). The Latin Vulgate rendered it lucifer, "light-bearer", which the KJV kept as a name. The taunt is aimed at the king of Babylon (14:4), but many Christians, comparing Luke 10:18, have seen in it the fall of Satan, whose pride the king's pride reflects. In 2 Peter 1:19 and Revelation 22:16 "morning star" is a title of Christ.

14:13.t: "The mount of assembly ... the utmost heights of the north": in ancient Near Eastern myth the gods met on a mountain in the far north. The king claims a place among the gods.

16:5.t: "In steadfast love a throne will be established" (Hebrew behesed): a promise of a king from David's house who rules by hesed and emet. Even in an oracle against Moab, Isaiah looks to the Messiah's reign as Moab's hope.

17:10.t: "God your Savior ... the Rock" (Hebrew elohe yish'ekh, tsur): Israel forgot the One who saved them. "Imported vines": literally "vines of a foreign god", perhaps garden shrines for fertility gods.

19:24.t: "Egypt My people ... Assyria the work of My hands": two of Israel's greatest enemies receive titles once given only to Israel. Isaiah looks ahead to the day when the nations will worship the LORD together with His people (see 2:2-4, 56:6-7).

21:9.t: "Babylon has fallen, has fallen!": echoed in Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 about the final fall of the world system that opposes God.

22:22.t: "The key to the house of David": the authority of the palace steward. Jesus applies this verse to Himself in Revelation 3:7, the One who holds all authority to open and shut.

24:5.t: "The everlasting covenant" (Hebrew berit olam): perhaps the covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:16), made with all humanity, which the whole earth has broken.

24:21.t: "The powers in the heavens above" (Hebrew tseva hammarom): literally "the host of the height", spiritual powers opposed to God. Compare Ephesians 6:12.

25:8.t: "He will swallow up death forever" (Hebrew bila hammavet lanetsach): Paul quotes this in 1 Corinthians 15:54, "Death is swallowed up in victory", following the Greek. Revelation 21:4 echoes "God will wipe away every tear".

26:3.t: "Perfect peace" (Hebrew shalom shalom): peace doubled, the fullest well-being. "Steadfast" (samukh): leaning on, supported by God.

27:1.t: "Leviathan" (Hebrew livyatan): see Job 41 and Psalm 74:14. The ancient sea monster stands for every power of chaos and evil; Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 call the dragon "that ancient serpent".

28:11.t: "With foreign lips and strange tongues": Assyrian invaders will speak to the people who refused to listen. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 14:21 about speaking in tongues.

28:16.t: "A precious cornerstone ... the one who relies on it" (Hebrew ha-ma'amin): "the one who believes". The New Testament applies this stone to Christ (Romans 9:33, 10:11, 1 Peter 2:6), following the Greek, "will never be put to shame". The KJV's "shall not make haste".

29:13.t: "Their hearts are far from Me": Jesus quotes this verse against the religious leaders of His day (Matthew 15:8-9, Mark 7:6-7).

29:14.t: "The wisdom of the wise will perish": Paul quotes this in 1 Corinthians 1:19.

29:16.t: "The potter ... the clay": see 45:9, 64:8, Jeremiah 18:1-6 and Romans 9:20-21.

30:15.t: "In repentance and rest" (Hebrew beshuvah vanachat): shuvah means "returning", turning back to God. The KJV's "In returning and rest". Salvation comes by turning to God and trusting Him, not by alliances or horses.

30:18.t: "The LORD longs to be gracious" (Hebrew yechakkeh): literally "waits", as the KJV has it. God waits eagerly for the moment He can show mercy; "Blessed are all who wait for Him" uses the same verb of the people.

32:1.t: "A king will reign in righteousness": a picture of the ideal king, fulfilled in the Messiah (9:6-7, 11:1-5).

32:15.t: "The Spirit is poured on us from on high": see 44:3, Joel 2:28 and Acts 2:17.

32:17.t: "The fruit of righteousness will be peace" (Hebrew shalom): see James 3:18.

33:14.t: "The consuming fire": the holiness of God, before whom no sinner can stand (Hebrews 12:29). Verses 15-16 answer the question, as Psalms 15 and 24 do.

33:17.t: "The King in His beauty": the LORD Himself, the true King (verse 22). The pronouns are capitalized.

35:4.t: "Your God will come ... to save you": verses 5-6 describe the miracles Jesus pointed to as signs that He was the One to come (Matthew 11:4-5).

35:8.t: "The Way of Holiness" (Hebrew derekh haqqodesh): a road for the redeemed returning to Zion. Compare 40:3 and John 14:6.

37:36.t: "The angel of the LORD" (Hebrew mal'akh YHWH): see Genesis 16:7. Sennacherib's own records boast of shutting Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" but do not claim to have taken Jerusalem.

38:17.t: "You have put all my sins behind Your back": God chooses not to look at them any longer. Compare Micah 7:19 and Psalm 103:12. "In Your love" (Hebrew chashaqta): God's love that holds fast, the same verb as in Deuteronomy 7:7.

40:31.t: "Wait for the LORD" (Hebrew qoye YHWH): the verb qavah means to wait with eager expectation and trust, from a word for a stretched, twisted cord. Those who hope in the LORD exchange their strength for His.

41:8.t: "Abraham My friend" (Hebrew ohavi): literally "the one who loves Me". James 2:23 calls Abraham "the friend of God".

41:14.t: "Your Redeemer" (Hebrew go'alekh): the kinsman who rescues a family member (see Exodus 6:6, Ruth 4). This title for God appears thirteen times in Isaiah 41-63.

42:1.t: The first "Servant Song" (with 49:1-6, 50:4-9 and 52:13-53:12). The Servant is sometimes Israel (41:8, 42:19), but in these songs He is an individual who fulfills Israel's calling and suffers for others. Matthew 12:18-21 applies 42:1-4 to Jesus, and at His baptism the Father's words echo verse 1 (Matthew 3:17). Following this reading, the Servant's pronouns are capitalized in the songs.

42:3.t: "A bruised reed He will not break": the Servant is gentle with the weak and failing.

42:6.t: "A light for the nations" (Hebrew or goyim): see 49:6, Luke 2:32 and Acts 13:47.

43:1.t: "I have redeemed you ... you are Mine" (Hebrew ge'altikha): God speaks as the kinsman-redeemer who owns and protects His family.

43:10.t: "I am He" (Hebrew ani hu): a claim to be the only true God, repeated in 41:4, 43:13, 46:4 and 48:12. The Greek translation renders it ego eimi, "I am", the words Jesus uses of Himself in John 8:24, 8:58 and 13:19.

45:7.t: "I bring prosperity and create disaster" (Hebrew shalom ... ra): the KJV's "I make peace, and create evil". Ra here means calamity, not moral evil; God is sovereign over good times and bad (compare Amos 3:6, Lamentations 3:38).

45:23.t: "Before Me every knee will bow": Paul applies this to Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11 and to God's judgment in Romans 14:11, showing that the honor due to the LORD alone belongs to Christ.

46:4.t: "I have made you and I will carry you" (Hebrew ani asiti va'ani essa): the idols must be carried; the LORD carries His people from birth to old age.

48:16.t: "The Lord GOD has sent me, endowed with His Spirit": the speaker is the prophet, or the Servant. Christians have noted the mention of the Lord, His Spirit and the One sent.

49:3.t: "You are My Servant, Israel": the Servant is called Israel because He embodies and fulfills what Israel was meant to be; yet He also has a mission to Israel (verses 5-6). Paul and Barnabas apply verse 6 to their mission to the Gentiles (Acts 13:47), and Simeon echoes it of the infant Jesus (Luke 2:32).

49:8.t: "In the time of My favor ... in the day of salvation": Paul quotes this in 2 Corinthians 6:2: "Now is the day of salvation."

49:15.t: "Though she may forget, I will not forget you ... engraved on the palms of My hands": God's love is stronger than a mother's. "Compassion" (rachem), from rechem, "womb"; see Exodus 34:6.

50:4.t: The third Servant Song. The Servant learns obedience daily and willingly endures beating and spitting, fulfilled in Jesus' trial (Matthew 26:67, 27:30). "Set my face like flint": compare Luke 9:51, where Jesus "resolutely set His face to go to Jerusalem".

50:8.t: "He who vindicates me is near ... Who will condemn me?": Paul echoes this in Romans 8:33-34.

52:15.t: "He will sprinkle many nations" (Hebrew yazzeh): the verb used for the priest sprinkling blood or water to cleanse (Leviticus 16:14). The Greek reads "many nations will marvel at Him".

53:4.t: "Our pain ... our sorrows" (Hebrew cholayenu ... makh'ovenu): literally "our sicknesses ... our pains", which the KJV renders "griefs" and "sorrows". Matthew 8:17 applies the verse to Jesus' healing ministry.

53:5.t: "Pierced" (Hebrew mecholal): wounded through, the KJV's "wounded". "Peace" (shalom): the Servant's punishment brings us wholeness and peace with God. "By His wounds" (chabburato): the welts of a beating, the KJV's "stripes". See 1 Peter 2:24.

53:6.t: "Laid on Him the iniquity of us all": the LORD made our guilt fall on Him, the heart of substitution. Compare Leviticus 16:21-22, where the sins are laid on the goat.

53:7.t: "Like a lamb to the slaughter": the Ethiopian official was reading these verses when Philip told him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32-35). John the Baptist called Jesus "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29).

53:9.t: "With the rich in His death": fulfilled when Jesus was buried in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man (Matthew 27:57-60).

53:10.t: "An offering for sin" (Hebrew asham): the guilt offering, which made restitution for wrong done (Leviticus 5:14-6:7). The Servant's life is the payment for others' guilt. "He will see His offspring and prolong His days": after death, the Servant lives, a pointer to resurrection.

53:12.t: "Was numbered with the transgressors": Jesus quotes this of Himself (Luke 22:37); He was crucified between two criminals and prayed for those who crucified Him (Luke 23:34).

54:8.t: "Everlasting kindness ... My steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed olam, chasdi): God's hesed outlasts the mountains. See Genesis 24:27.

54:10.t: "Everlasting kindness ... My steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed olam, chasdi): God's hesed outlasts the mountains. See Genesis 24:27.

55:1.t: "Without money and without cost": God's invitation is a free gift. Compare John 7:37 and Revelation 22:17.

55:3.t: "My faithful love promised to David" (Hebrew chasde david hanne'emanim): the KJV's "the sure mercies of David", God's hesed promised to David's line (2 Samuel 7:15-16). Paul quotes it in Acts 13:34 as fulfilled in the risen Christ.

55:11.t: "My word ... will not return to Me empty": the Hebrew reqam means "empty-handed". God's word always does its work.

57:15.t: "Contrite" (Hebrew dakka): literally "crushed". The God who lives in the highest heaven also lives with the broken and humble. Compare Psalm 51:17.

58:6.t: "The kind of fasting I have chosen": true worship is shown in justice and mercy, not in religious ritual alone. Compare Micah 6:8, Matthew 25:35-36 and James 1:27.

59:17.t: "Righteousness as His breastplate, and the helmet of salvation": Paul draws on this verse for the armor of God given to believers (Ephesians 6:14-17, 1 Thessalonians 5:8).

60:1.t: "Arise, shine, for your light has come": the light is the glory of the LORD Himself. Revelation 21:23-26 uses verses 3, 11 and 19-20 to describe the new Jerusalem.

61:1.t: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me": in the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read this passage and said, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:18-21). He stopped before "the day of vengeance", which awaits His return. "The year of the LORD's favor" recalls the Year of Jubilee, when slaves were freed and land restored (Leviticus 25:10).

61:10.t: "Garments of salvation ... a robe of righteousness": God Himself clothes His people in righteousness. Compare Zechariah 3:4, Galatians 3:27 and Revelation 19:8.

63:9.t: "In all their distress He too was distressed": the KJV reads "In all their affliction he was afflicted", following the Hebrew reading with lo ("to Him"); the written text has lo' ("not"). "The angel of His presence": literally "the angel of His face".

63:10.t: "His Holy Spirit" (Hebrew ruach qodsho): one of only three times this exact phrase occurs in the Old Testament (with Psalm 51:11). The Spirit can be "grieved", a personal response; Paul echoes this in Ephesians 4:30.

63:16.t: "You are our Father": one of the rare places in the Old Testament where Israel addresses God as Father (also 64:8).

64:4.t: "No eye has seen any God besides You": Paul draws on this verse in 1 Corinthians 2:9.

64:8.t: "We are the clay, You are the potter": see 29:16 and 45:9.

65:17.t: "New heavens and a new earth" (Hebrew shamayim chadashim va'arets chadashah): God's final renewal of all creation. 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1-4 take up this promise.

66:24.t: "The worms ... will not die, the fire ... will not be quenched": Jesus uses these words to describe hell (Gehenna) in Mark 9:48. In Jewish synagogue reading, verse 23 is repeated after verse 24 so that the book does not end on judgment.
